props.title: The Big Hit
props.initialSlug: Hit man's perfect life crumbles in zany kidnap plot

sections.content: The Big Hit (1998) represents a fascinating moment when Hong Kong action cinema's influence crashed into late-90s Hollywood swagger. Director Che-Kirk Wong, fresh from Hong Kong, brings John Woo-style gunplay to a distinctly American crime comedy. Like Grosse Pointe Blank (1997) and Get Shorty (1995), it plays with the hitman-with-heart trope, but adds hyperkinetic action sequences that clearly echo Hard Boiled (1992) and The Killer (1989). Mark Wahlberg's Melvin Smiley embodies this cultural fusion - a Jewish hitman who's pathologically nice, does pilates, and can shoot two guns while doing backflips.

sections.content: The film's timing is crucial - it landed right when Hollywood was desperately trying to replicate Hong Kong action magic. Rush Hour (1998) and Romeo Must Die (2000) were part of this wave, but The Big Hit takes bigger stylistic risks. The action sequences, choreographed by Hong Kong veteran Xin Xin Xiong, deliver the goods with wire-assisted acrobatics and bullet ballets. Yet it's wrapped in distinctly American late-90s comedy, complete with video store subplot and Lou Diamond Phillips hamming it up gloriously as a betrayed criminal partner.

What makes The Big Hit particularly interesting is how it predates the full mainstreaming of Asian action aesthetics that would come with The Matrix (1999) and Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon (2000). It's a bridge film, sometimes awkward but fascinating, showing Hollywood learning to absorb Hong Kong cinema's influence. The movie's mix of tones - from broad comedy to brutal action - reflects this cultural fusion, even when it doesn't entirely work. SUBHEAD: Action Comedy Evolution

sections.content: Looking at The Big Hit through today's lens, you can see how it influenced later action-comedies. The self-aware hitman character type evolved through films like Mr. & Mrs. Smith (2005) and Lucky Number Slevin (2006). Its rapid-fire editing and kinetic camera moves became standard language for action sequences, though few matched its gleeful excess. Even the film's multicultural cast and genre-blending approach feels ahead of its time, predating the international action film boom of the 2000s.
